difficultyReason: Two-concept conditional gap: stimulus links 'board-certified' to 'eligible for hospital privileges' and 'eligible for hospital privileges' to 'covered by the malpractice policy,' but the conclusion jumps to coverage; students must identify the missing conditional chain link rather than a one-step bridge.
stimulus: Only physicians who are board-certified are eligible for hospital privileges at Westbrook Medical Center. Every physician who is eligible for hospital privileges at Westbrook is covered under the center's group malpractice policy. Dr. Reyes is board-certified. Therefore, Dr. Reyes is covered under Westbrook's group malpractice policy.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every physician who is covered under Westbrook's group malpractice policy is board-certified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Reyes is eligible for hospital privileges at Westbrook Medical Center.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some physicians who are board-certified are not covered under any malpractice policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No physician is covered under Westbrook's group malpractice policy unless that physician practices internal medicine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians who are not board-certified may still be covered under some malpractice policies.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes: board-certified → eligible for privileges → covered by policy. Dr. Reyes is board-certified, but the first conditional goes from 'only board-certified are eligible' — which means eligible → board-certified, not board-certified → eligible. Adding B (Dr. Reyes is eligible) directly bridges her into the second conditional, forcing the conclusion that she is covered. With B in place, the chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: This reverses the second conditional (covered → board-certified instead of board-certified → covered). Reversed-conditional trap: it does not establish that board-certified physicians are covered.
explanations.C: This weakens rather than closes the gap, suggesting board-certified physicians might lack coverage — the opposite of what is needed.
explanations.D: Introduces a new restriction (internal medicine) not present in the premises, which would actually undermine the conclusion rather than support it.
explanations.E: This addresses physicians who are NOT board-certified, which is irrelevant to Dr. Reyes, who is board-certified.

difficultyReason: Two-step conditional gap in an economics context. The stimulus introduces 'price controls' and 'market distortions,' then concludes about 'reduced investment.' Students must supply the link between distortions and investment — a non-obvious but not deeply nested bridge.
stimulus: Economists agree that whenever a government imposes strict price controls on essential goods, those controls inevitably produce significant market distortions. The government of Caldoria has just imposed strict price controls on fuel. Consequently, investment in Caldoria's energy sector will decline.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Significant market distortions always lead to a decline in investment in the affected sector.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Investment in Caldoria's energy sector was already low before the price controls were imposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Governments that impose price controls on essential goods usually do so for political rather than economic reasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some market distortions in the energy sector can eventually be corrected without reducing investment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fuel is not considered an essential good in some economic models.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: strict price controls → significant market distortions. The conclusion is: investment in Caldoria's energy sector will decline. Choice A supplies the missing universal conditional: significant market distortions → decline in investment. Combined with the premise chain, this forces the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.B: Prior investment levels are not the gap the argument needs to close; they are irrelevant to whether distortions cause decline.
explanations.C: The motivation behind imposing controls is irrelevant to whether investment will decline as a result.
explanations.D: This is a partial concession that actually weakens the link from distortions to declining investment rather than closing it.
explanations.E: Weakens the argument by questioning whether fuel qualifies as an essential good, rather than bridging the gap to the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in an environmental science context. The stimulus connects 'deforestation above threshold' to 'watershed instability' and needs a bridge to the conclusion about 'municipal water shortages.' Moderate distractor density with a reversed-conditional trap.
stimulus: Environmental scientists have established that when deforestation in a river basin exceeds forty percent of the forested area, the basin's watershed becomes unstable. The Korvenna River basin has now lost more than forty percent of its forested area to logging. The city of Aldenmoor, which draws all of its water from the Korvenna River, will therefore face a shortage of potable water.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cities that draw water from unstable watersheds always face shortages of potable water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldenmoor has never invested in water-purification infrastructure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some cities that face shortages of potable water are located near unstable watersheds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Watershed instability in the Korvenna basin is caused exclusively by logging.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unstable watersheds sometimes recover if deforestation is halted immediately.

explanations.correct: The premises yield: deforestation > 40% → watershed unstable; Korvenna basin has lost > 40% → Korvenna watershed is unstable; Aldenmoor draws all water from Korvenna. Choice A supplies the universal conditional needed: city draws from unstable watershed → faces potable water shortage. This closes the gap and forces the conclusion with necessity.
explanations.B: Purification infrastructure is a new concept not present in the premises; even with purification, the link from instability to shortage is not established.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'some cities' establishes only a partial correlation, not the universal link needed to force the conclusion.
explanations.D: The cause of the instability is not the gap; the gap is between instability and the shortage conclusion.
explanations.E: This is irrelevant to whether Aldenmoor will face a shortage now; potential recovery does not close the inferential gap.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in a law/policy context. The stimulus establishes a legislative rule about 'conflicts of interest' and 'recusal,' then concludes a specific official must recuse herself. Students must bridge the official's situation to the conflict-of-interest category.
stimulus: Under the Harwick municipal code, any official who holds a financial interest in a company that is the subject of a pending regulatory decision must recuse herself from voting on that decision. Councilmember Draven holds stock in Meridian Logistics, and the council is currently deliberating a zoning variance that would directly affect Meridian Logistics. Therefore, Councilmember Draven must recuse herself from the vote.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Holding stock in a company constitutes holding a financial interest in that company.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Councilmember Draven was aware that Meridian Logistics had a pending regulatory matter before the council.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No official who recuses herself from a vote may later cast a vote on any related matter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The zoning variance would benefit Meridian Logistics financially.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Officials who recuse themselves from votes on conflicts of interest are praised by ethics watchdog groups.

explanations.correct: The municipal code requires recusal for any official who 'holds a financial interest' in the company. The premises state Draven holds stock. Choice A bridges these: stock-holding = financial interest. With this assumption, Draven satisfies the code's condition and must recuse herself — the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.B: Awareness is not a condition stated in the municipal code; the code's recusal requirement does not depend on the official's knowledge.
explanations.C: This introduces a further restriction about future votes, which is irrelevant to whether Draven must recuse herself now.
explanations.D: Whether the variance would benefit Meridian financially is not what the code requires — it requires a financial interest in the company, not proof of directional benefit.
explanations.E: External praise from watchdog groups is irrelevant to the logical necessity of recusal under the municipal code.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in a technology context. The stimulus links 'unencrypted transmission' to 'interception risk' and 'interception risk' to 'data breach,' but the conclusion states the company is 'in violation of its security protocol.' The missing link between data breach risk and protocol violation must be supplied.
stimulus: Tessatech's internal security protocol states that any data transmission carrying personal client information must be encrypted. An audit revealed that several of Tessatech's servers have been transmitting client data without encryption. Any unencrypted transmission of personal data creates a risk of unauthorized interception. Therefore, Tessatech is in violation of its own security protocol.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tessatech's security protocol was drafted by external cybersecurity consultants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transmitting personal client information without encryption violates Tessatech's security protocol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any company that faces a risk of unauthorized interception is liable under data-protection law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encrypted transmissions occasionally carry a risk of unauthorized interception as well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tessatech's clients were informed that their data might be transmitted without encryption.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that (1) Tessatech's protocol requires encryption for client data, and (2) several servers transmitted client data without encryption. Choice B directly bridges these to the conclusion: transmitting personal client information without encryption = violating the protocol. With B, the conclusion follows necessarily from the audit finding.
explanations.A: Who drafted the protocol is irrelevant to whether transmitting unencrypted data violates it.
explanations.C: Legal liability under data-protection law is a separate issue from whether Tessatech violated its own internal protocol.
explanations.D: Risks associated with encrypted transmissions do not bear on whether unencrypted transmissions violate the protocol.
explanations.E: Client notification does not determine whether Tessatech violated its own security protocol.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in a history/ethics context. The stimulus introduces a principle about 'collective punishment' and 'moral illegitimacy,' then applies it to a historical event; students must supply the link between the specific policy and the category of collective punishment.
stimulus: Any policy that imposes suffering on individuals solely because of their membership in a group, rather than because of anything those individuals have done, is an instance of collective punishment and is therefore morally illegitimate. The internment policy carried out during the Second World War against Japanese-American citizens imposed suffering on those citizens solely because of their ethnic heritage. Therefore, that internment policy was morally illegitimate.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Policies that are morally illegitimate should always be repealed as quickly as possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ethnic heritage is a form of group membership.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Collective punishment is wrong only when it targets ethnic minorities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The internment policy was the result of widespread racial prejudice rather than genuine security concerns.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Morally illegitimate policies always cause greater suffering than the policies they replace.

explanations.correct: The general principle covers suffering imposed 'because of membership in a group.' The premise states the internment was based on 'ethnic heritage.' For the principle to apply, ethnic heritage must qualify as group membership. Choice B supplies exactly this bridge, forcing the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.A: What should be done about morally illegitimate policies is outside the scope of the argument's conclusion, which is only about whether the policy was illegitimate.
explanations.C: This narrows the principle to ethnic minorities, which would actually weaken the generality of the argument rather than complete it.
explanations.D: The motivation behind the policy (prejudice vs. security) is not the gap; the gap is whether ethnic heritage constitutes group membership under the principle.
explanations.E: Comparative suffering is irrelevant to whether the policy qualifies as morally illegitimate under the stated principle.

difficultyReason: Two-concept conditional gap in a linguistics context. The stimulus bridges 'phonemic inventory reduction' to 'language contact,' then concludes about dialect merger; students must supply the link between contact-driven inventory reduction and merger, resisting a reversed-conditional distractor.
stimulus: Linguists have found that whenever two dialects of the same language come into sustained contact, each dialect's phonemic inventory tends to undergo reduction. Sociolinguists have documented that the northern and southern dialects of Varennic have been in sustained contact for the past three generations. Therefore, linguists should expect the northern and southern dialects of Varennic to eventually merge into a single dialect.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any two dialects whose phonemic inventories have undergone reduction due to sustained contact will eventually merge into a single dialect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dialects that merge into a single dialect always share identical phonemic inventories beforehand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phonemic inventory reduction is the only linguistic change that results from sustained dialect contact.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some dialects that undergo phonemic inventory reduction do not merge with other dialects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The northern dialect of Varennic has a larger phonemic inventory than the southern dialect.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: sustained contact → phonemic inventory reduction; northern and southern Varennic dialects have been in sustained contact → their inventories have undergone reduction. Choice A supplies the final conditional: phonemic inventory reduction due to sustained contact → eventual dialect merger. This completes the chain and forces the conclusion.
explanations.B: This is the reversed conditional (merged dialects had identical inventories), which runs backward and does not force the forward conclusion that reduction leads to merger.
explanations.C: Whether inventory reduction is the only change is irrelevant; the question is whether it leads to merger.
explanations.D: This actually undermines the conclusion by allowing that reduction does not guarantee merger — the opposite of what is needed.
explanations.E: The relative sizes of the phonemic inventories are irrelevant to whether the dialects will merge.

difficultyReason: Two-step gap in a policy/environmental science context. The stimulus links 'carbon tax' to 'emission reductions' and needs the bridge to 'treaty compliance.' Moderate distractor density including a too-weak answer and a partial-bridge trap.
stimulus: The Nordenvaal climate treaty requires every signatory nation to reduce its industrial carbon emissions by at least fifteen percent within ten years. Economic analysts have demonstrated that a sufficiently high carbon tax is the only policy instrument that can guarantee a fifteen-percent reduction in industrial carbon emissions within a decade. Ruland, a signatory to the Nordenvaal treaty, has just enacted such a carbon tax. Ruland will therefore comply with the Nordenvaal treaty's emission-reduction requirement.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any nation that achieves at least a fifteen-percent reduction in industrial carbon emissions within ten years satisfies the Nordenvaal treaty's emission-reduction requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ruland's carbon tax is likely to reduce industrial emissions by more than fifteen percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nations that comply with the Nordenvaal treaty tend to benefit economically in the long run.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carbon taxes are the most popular policy instrument among Nordenvaal signatories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some nations that enact carbon taxes do not achieve the required emission reductions.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that (1) the treaty requires a 15% reduction, (2) a sufficiently high carbon tax guarantees a 15% reduction, and (3) Ruland enacted such a tax. This means Ruland will achieve a 15% reduction. Choice A supplies the final bridge: achieving the 15% reduction = satisfying the treaty requirement. The conclusion then follows necessarily.
explanations.B: Too weak: 'likely to reduce by more than fifteen percent' is probabilistic, not universal, and does not force the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.C: Long-term economic benefits are irrelevant to whether Ruland satisfies the treaty's emission requirement.
explanations.D: The popularity of carbon taxes among signatories does not bear on whether Ruland's enactment satisfies the treaty.
explanations.E: This undermines the argument by suggesting the carbon tax might not work, which is the opposite of what is needed.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in an arts context with a refutation structure. The stimulus cites a specific artist to refute a critical claim; students must supply the conditional that connects the artist's properties to the refutation, resisting a subject-shift trap.
stimulus: Several art critics have argued that any painter who works exclusively in a nonrepresentational style cannot produce work that is emotionally accessible to general audiences. This claim is mistaken. Consider Vera Solano, a painter whose entire body of work is nonrepresentational and who has drawn overwhelmingly positive emotional responses from gallery visitors with no specialized training in art.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No painter who draws positive emotional responses from untrained gallery visitors works in a representational style.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any painter who produces work that draws positive emotional responses from untrained audiences produces work that is emotionally accessible to general audiences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vera Solano is widely regarded as the most important nonrepresentational painter of her generation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Painters who work in both representational and nonrepresentational styles are more emotionally accessible than those who work in only one style.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The emotional accessibility of a painting is determined primarily by its color palette rather than its representational content.

explanations.correct: To refute the critics' claim, the argument needs to show that Solano — a nonrepresentational painter — produces emotionally accessible work. The premises show she gets positive emotional responses from untrained gallery visitors. Choice B bridges this to the critics' specific vocabulary: positive emotional responses from untrained audiences = emotional accessibility to general audiences. With B, the counterexample is complete and the critics' claim is definitively refuted.
explanations.A: This is the reversed conditional — it says painters with positive responses don't work representationally, running backward from the needed direction.
explanations.C: Solano's reputation or standing among peers does not establish that her work is emotionally accessible to general audiences in the critics' sense.
explanations.D: This introduces a comparison between painters who use both styles, which is irrelevant to refuting the claim about exclusively nonrepresentational painters.
explanations.E: This principle-wrapping trap invokes color palette as a determining factor, but even if true, it does not force the conclusion that Solano's work is emotionally accessible in the required sense.

difficultyReason: Two-step gap in a medicine/ethics context. The stimulus links 'experimental treatment' to 'informed consent requirement' and needs a bridge to the conclusion about a specific clinical trial's status. Moderate distractor density with a partial-bridge trap and a too-weak trap.
stimulus: Under medical ethics guidelines, any experimental treatment administered to human subjects without their informed consent constitutes a violation of patient autonomy. Researchers at Galloway Institute administered a novel drug compound to participants in a clinical trial. Several participants later reported that they had not been told the compound was experimental at the time they enrolled. Therefore, the Galloway Institute trial constitutes a violation of patient autonomy.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who were not informed that a treatment is experimental have not given informed consent to that treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Violations of patient autonomy in clinical trials should result in the immediate suspension of the trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Galloway Institute researchers were aware that some participants had not been told the compound was experimental.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Informed consent procedures at the Galloway Institute are generally less rigorous than industry standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some participants in the Galloway trial may have consented to receive an experimental treatment under a different name.

explanations.correct: The ethics guideline states: experimental treatment + no informed consent → violation of patient autonomy. The premises establish the treatment was experimental and that several participants were not told it was experimental. Choice A supplies the definitional bridge: not being told the treatment is experimental = not giving informed consent. This closes the gap and forces the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.B: What should happen after a violation is identified is irrelevant to whether the trial constitutes a violation in the first place.
explanations.C: The researchers' awareness (scienter) is not a condition in the ethics guideline; the guideline requires only that consent was absent, not that researchers knew it was absent.
explanations.D: Comparative rigor of consent procedures is a partial bridge at best — it suggests the institute may have failed to obtain consent but does not establish with necessity that the specific participants lacked informed consent.
explanations.E: This actually undermines the conclusion by suggesting some participants may have consented under different conditions, which is the opposite of what the argument needs.
